newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China's October fuel oil imports up, diesel stalls.
newsitem.headline: China's October fuel oil imports up, diesel stalls.

text.p: China's fuel oil imports are seen rising in October as domestic stocks fall, but diesel imports are likely to level off because China's own production is going up, traders said on Wednesday.
China's fuel oil imports in October were expected to reach 300,000 tonnes, up from just over 200,000 tonnes in September.
Traders from China's state oil refiner, SINOCHEM, told Reuters higher imports were being encouraged by current low domestic stocks and declining international spot market prices.

"Previous high fuel oil prices in late August and early September in the benchmark Singapore market have caused Chinese buyers to turn away from imports, relying more on domestic inventories," a trader in Hong Kong told Reuters.
Benchmark fuel oil prices jumped $22 per tonne, rising from $92.50 per tonne in mid-August to $114.50 on September 3.

During the Gulf tensions between Iraq and the United States which started on September 3, prices were volatile, traders said. But with the tension easing, prices are showing signs of softening with more supplies available in the region, especially from South Korea and Singapore. Prices have stabilised at around $113.50.
China was expected to import more of its fuel oil from Japan and South Korea and less from Singapore to save on freight costs, traders at SINOCHEM said.

"Freight costs between South Korea and China are pegged at $7.50, a dollar lower from the charges between Singapore and China," a SINOCHEM trader said. "We will import at least 60,000 tonnes from Japan," he said.
Low domestic fuel oil output has also spurred more Chinese fuel oil imports, traders in Singapore said.

Traders point to figures released by China's State Statistical bureau -- that fuel oil output was 15.52 million tonnes in the first eight months of 1996, down around 19 percent compared with the same period last year.
Domestic production of diesel, or gasoil, is rising, however.
"China is gradually boosting its gas oil production at the expense of fuel oil as its domestic gas oil output was lagging far behind demand," said a SINOCHEM trader.
State refiner SINOPEC said China's fuel oil production in September and October was expected to be stable at around 1.81 million tonnes a month.
Current diesel output was up around 14 percent over last year, traders in SINOCHEM said.
China is forecast to import 200,000 to 300,000 tonnes of diesel in October, compared to the usual average of 400,000 to 500,000 tonnes per month, SINOCHEM traders told Reuters.
Traders in Singapore said China had bought several September cargoes of diesel when prices in Singapore were still high because of the U.S.-Iraq tensions.
Diesel was quoted in the Singapore spot market at an all-time high of $28.40 per tonne on September 13. Prices have since fallen by close to a dollar, but were still deemed high by Chinese buyers.
Traders at SINPOPEC said imports would not be cost effective because of low domestic retail prices.
The sources said SINOPEC wanted to raise its ex-refinery diesel prices, but that China's state planners were unlikely to grant approval soon.
